preamble: Assibilation of the palatalized stop [dʲ] to the voiced alveolo-palatal affricate [dʑ], keeping the palatal place while adding a fricative release. Shtokavian Serbo-Croatian turned the Proto-Slavic palatalized stop *ď into đ /dʑ/: *meďa 'border' > mèđa /měd͡ʑa/, *pręďa 'yarn' > pređa /prêd͡ʑa/. Polish has two [dʲ] inputs with different outcomes: the inherited Proto-Slavic *ď became dz (miedza, see the [dz] cell), while the dentals secondarily softened before front vowels became ć, dź in the 12th century, so softened [dʲ] gave dź [dʑ]: dzień /ˈd͡ʑɛɲ/ 'day', chodzić /ˈxɔ.d͡ʑit͡ɕ/ 'to walk' (cf. Russian день [dʲenʲ], ходить [xɐˈdʲitʲ] with the stop kept).

examples.note: Single palatalized *ď, not the earlier *dj cluster; contrast Macedonian меѓа, Polish miedza, Ukrainian межа.
Dialectal and rare; the usual words are čađa and saža.

examples.from: Proto-Slavic *dьnь, with [dʲ] softened before the front yer (cf. Russian день [dʲenʲ])
examples.note: Soft *t, *d became ć, dź in the 12th century.

examples.from: Old Polish chodzić, with softened [dʲ] before i (cf. Russian ходить [xɐˈdʲitʲ])
